title: The Black-Friday Cluster

scenario.situation: To prepare for the holiday spike, the lead wants to provision a large fixed processing cluster sized for peak load and keep it running through the season.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The lead believes a permanently provisioned, peak-sized cluster is the safe way to survive the holiday spike.
scenario.question: Is a fixed peak-sized cluster the right way to handle the spike, or does the load shape call for something else?

decisions.prompt: How do you approach capacity for the season?

options.label: Provision the fixed peak-sized cluster for the season
options.detail: Stand up peak capacity and keep it running through the holidays.
options.consequence: You stand up peak capacity and leave it running for months — paying for the busiest hour around the clock before checking what the load actually looks like the rest of the time.
options.divergenceCost: Sized standing capacity to the peak before profiling how often the peak occurs.

options.label: Profile the load shape over time — how peaky, and for how long
options.detail: Chart hourly demand across a representative period before choosing a capacity model.
options.consequence: You chart hourly load across a representative week: demand sits near a low baseline most of the day and spikes to ~8x for a few hours during evening promotions and event days. The peak is real but brief; most hours need a fraction of peak capacity.

options.label: Copy last year's cluster size
options.detail: Reuse the capacity that got you through last season.
options.consequence: You reuse last year's number without checking whether traffic, load shape, or the workload changed — anchoring capacity to a figure that may no longer fit.
options.divergenceCost: Reused last year's fixed size without reprofiling this year's load shape.

options.label: Size for the average load to save money
options.detail: Provision to the mean demand to keep costs down.
options.consequence: Sizing to the average guarantees you fall over during the very spikes the season is about — the opposite failure, trading a cost problem for an outage.
options.divergenceCost: Sized to the average, leaving no capacity for the spikes that define the season.

decisions.prompt: You've profiled the load shape. Which reading tells you whether fixed provisioning fits?

artifact.title: Peak capacity needed (units)
artifact.caption: Peak demand is up ~30% — the number the fixed cluster would be sized to. But peak alone says nothing about how many hours you'd actually use it.

options.label: The peak load figure
options.detail: Size the cluster to the highest demand you expect.
options.consequence: Sizing to the peak guarantees you never fall over — and guarantees you pay for that peak 24 hours a day when you only hit it for a few. The single peak number, read alone, always argues for over-provisioning.
options.divergenceCost: Sized to the peak in isolation, ignoring how few hours the peak actually lasts.

options.label: The full load distribution — peak-to-median ratio and hours near peak
options.detail: Look at how the whole day's demand is distributed, not just its maximum.
options.consequence: The distribution tells the real story: load is at or above 80% of peak for only ~3 hours a day; the median hour needs ~1/8 of peak capacity. A fixed peak-sized cluster would sit ~85% idle. Autoscaling that follows the curve matches spend to load and still absorbs the spike.

artifact.title: Hours per day at each load level
artifact.caption: The cluster would run at peak capacity 24h/day to serve a spike that lasts ~3h. Autoscaling to the load curve keeps the peak headroom while paying baseline rates the other 21 hours.

options.label: Approve the fixed peak-sized cluster for safety
options.detail: Guarantee capacity by running peak-sized hardware all season.
options.consequence: You buy certainty against the spike by paying peak rates around the clock — roughly 8x the compute you use in a typical hour, idle most of the day. Safe, but a large standing bill for capacity that's mostly unused.
options.divergenceCost: Bought around-the-clock peak capacity to cover a spike that lasts a few hours a day.

options.label: Recommend autoscaling / serverless with a floor and headroom, load-test the spike
options.detail: Let capacity track the curve, name the tradeoffs, and pre-warm ahead of known peaks.
options.consequence: You recommend elastic capacity — autoscaling with a sensible floor and burst headroom, or a serverless engine — so cost tracks the load curve. You flag the tradeoffs (scale-up lag, cold starts) and mitigate them by pre-warming ahead of known promo windows and load-testing the spike. Peak is covered; the other 21 hours cost baseline.

insight: The load was spiky, not sustained: demand hit peak for only about three hours a day and sat near an eighth of peak the rest of the time, so a fixed peak-sized cluster would have run ~85% idle around the clock. The lone peak figure, read in isolation, always argues for over-provisioning; the full load distribution — peak-to-median ratio and hours spent near peak — is what reveals whether fixed capacity fits. The lesson is to size to the shape of the load, not its maximum: elastic autoscaling or serverless matches spend to demand and still absorbs the spike, as long as you account for scale-up latency and pre-warm ahead of known peaks.
